issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' is hard to reconcile with simultaneously becoming so overwhelmed on recall that she has to stop and experiencing intense rage when remembering. Mild coexistence is possible, but 'very easily' directly opposes marked emotional disorganization on recall and is clinically inconsistent within the same node.

issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy 'Avoid Police' is poorly aligned with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a combat trauma in a 21-year-old nurse, avoidance of police is not supported by the listed triggers, threat items, or memory content, which center on sirens, bodily arousal, transport, flashbacks, scanning, and rage/overwhelm. This looks like a strategy targeting a threat context not otherwise represented in the formulation or symptom profile.

Avoiding police is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a combat trauma survivor who is a nurse. The other selected items center on alarm, flashbacks, sirens, somatic arousal, and generalized danger scanning, but nothing else suggests police-specific threat, authority-related trauma meaning, or a law-enforcement context. This strategy appears disconnected from the trigger, threat, and memory content.

Bus riding as a selected trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear clinical link to the other chosen items. The active formulation strongly links triggers with threat and maladaptive strategies, yet the other trigger items are sirens and heart racing, and the threat/memory items emphasize flashbacking, rage, overwhelm, and danger scanning without any transport-related cueing. As selected here, this item feels insufficiently anchored to the rest of the combat-related profile.

vignette:
Three years ago, during her deployment as a combat medic, Mia was riding in a Humvee that hit an IED. The blast flipped the vehicle, and the next few minutes were a nightmare of screaming, smoke, and blood. She remembered the high-pitched wail of the sirens from the medevac chopper that landed too late for the driver, and the sharp crack of small-arms fire as the ambush continued. Her own heart pounded so hard she could feel it in her throat. What stayed with her most was the rage—a hot, helpless fury at the insurgents, at the chaos, at the fact that nothing she did could save him. When she tried to tell the debriefing officer later, the words wouldn't come; the memory was a solid block of emotion that silenced her.

Back home, Mia began working as an emergency-room nurse, and the triggers were everywhere. The first time an ambulance siren wailed outside the hospital, she froze mid-step, her heart suddenly racing, and she found herself scanning every corner of the hallway for cover. After that, she started avoiding the ambulance bay altogether, taking the long way through the hospital to stay away from the sirens that made her feel like she was back in that burning vehicle. Even loud noises on the ward—a dropped metal tray, a slamming door—could send her into a defensive crouch, and she learned to predict where such sounds came from so she could brace herself. She had come to believe that any unexpected loud noise might be the start of an attack, so she avoided the break room during shift changes and ate lunch alone in a supply closet. Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been.

The memory itself operated like a trap. When it surfaced, usually triggered by a siren or her own pounding heart after a code blue, Mia was flooded with that same rage—a fury so intense she sometimes had to grip the counter and bite her cheek to keep from shouting. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore. The overwhelm was so complete that she would stand paralysed, unable to find the words to tell her colleagues she was okay. The memory also made her hypervigilant: after a flashback, she would spend the rest of her shift scanning every patient's room, every corridor, certain that danger was about to break through the hospital doors. Conversely, her constant scanning—a threat-driven habit—kept her memory alive; every time she checked a corner or listened for approaching footsteps, she was reminded of scanning for the enemy in the desert.

The cycles tightened. When her boyfriend suggested they go for a run together, Mia refused—exercise made her heart race, and a racing heart meant she was in danger, which meant she couldn't stop scanning. Avoiding exercise left her restless and irritable, and on nights when she stayed in to avoid the gym, she would lie awake replaying the explosion. She also began to avoid positive events. Her boyfriend planned a surprise dinner, and instead of feeling happy, she felt a spike of fear: happiness felt like letting her guard down, and letting her guard down was how you got ambushed. The threat of feeling good seemed so dangerous that she snapped at him, pushing him away. In turn, her own aggression frightened her, and the flash of rage she saw in herself triggered the memory of her anger during the ambush, which left her more overwhelmed and less able to speak.

At work, her irritability became a problem. A loud noise in the trauma bay would set off a flashback, and after the flashback she would be short-tempered with the nursing assistants, snapping at them for rearranging equipment. The outbursts led her to avoid the unit altogether, too ashamed to face her colleagues, and avoidance meant she spent more time isolated, which gave her more space to ruminate on the memory. The constant checking of her surroundings made her exhausted, but she couldn't stop—every time she looked over her shoulder, she felt a little of the rage from the past leak into the present.

What finally brought Mia to a therapist was a panicked call from her boyfriend after she shoved him away during a cuddle. She had heard a distant siren through the window, her heart jumped, and before she knew it she was pushing him off the couch, scanning the room for a weapon, her fists clenched. The look on his face was terror, and for a moment she saw herself through his eyes—a threat instead of a partner. That night, for the first time, she desperately wanted to explain, but the words wouldn't come, and the overwhelming shame made her feel like she was suffocating. She is terrified that she will hurt him again, or that the hospital will finally fire her, and she is hoping that if she can just find a way to describe what happened—to turn the block of emotion into a story—she might finally stop fighting everyone who tries to get close.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows triggers causing the memory, but never that the memory itself causes triggers to appear.
The vignette shows triggers causing threat and threat causing maladaptive strategies, but never that threat causes triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers causing the memory, but never that the memory itself causes triggers to appear.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers causing threat and threat causing maladaptive strategies, but never that threat causes triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
